docs.title: About SIGGD
docs.text:
Founded in Fall 2011, Purdue ACM's Special Interest Group on Game Development is a multi-disciplinary group of Purdue University students that creates a new game each school year. As part of the Association for Computing Machinery Purdue chapter, we are the first SIGGD of ACM National. Our goal is to develop creative and interesting games. In addition, we host a game jam (game development hackathon) each semester where groups come together either online or in-person to create a video game prototype in 48 hours.

  We primarily communicate through our Discord Server, so if you are interested in joining the club be sure to join that to get started!

Before submitting a PR, run mkdocs build --strict to catch broken links and nav errors. Every new page also needs an entry in the nav: section of mkdocs.yml.

Documenting a project's code? Codebase pages describe one release of the game and are updated every milestone. Their extra rules, such as pinned source links and a milestone banner, are under "Codebase docs" in the Style Guide. The 26-27 Game Milestones page has the checklist for moving the docs to a new milestone.

Prefer working in Google Docs? You can embed a Google Doc, Sheet, Slides deck, or Form instead of writing Markdown, either as a whole page or inside a normal one. The doc stays live, so edits show up on the site right away. Put the file in the SIGGD Shared Drive, set sharing to "Anyone with the link", and follow the Google Doc Template.

Author attribution is automatic via git history. Make sure your name is set:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@email.com"

If you're committing content someone else wrote, add author: "@their-username" to the page frontmatter. They get credited as the original author; you show as the editor.

docs.title: Style Guide
docs.text:
Looking for how to write code?

This page is about writing docs. For how we write C# in the game, see the C# Style Guide.

Voice: Write in second person ("you") or imperative, active voice, and keep it concise. This is a club wiki, so feel free to be casual! Contractions and the occasional "I" are totally fine.

Frontmatter: Every page needs at minimum a title. Add author: "@username" only when committing someone else's work.

---
title: "Page Title"
tags:
  - relevant-tag
---

---
title: "Page Title"
author: "@github-username"   # committing someone else's work
---

For tutorials, also add difficulty, time_estimate, and prerequisites.

Google Docs: Embed a Google Doc, Sheet, Slides deck, or Form with google_doc in the frontmatter (a whole page), or by tagging a link with { .google-doc } (inside a page). Both take the normal Share → Copy link URL, and height overrides the default size. Full instructions, including sharing and where files should live, are in the Google Doc Template.

---
title: "Story Design Doc"
google_doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit?usp=sharing
---

[Story Design Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit){ .google-doc }

Codebase docs: Pages under a project's codebase/ folder describe one release of the game, and the Codebase Template has their full layout. They also follow these rules:

  • Pin source links to a release tag, never to main: https://github.com/PurdueSIGGD/<repo>/blob/v0.1.0/Assets/.... Add #L42 to link one line. A link to main drifts as soon as someone pushes.

  • Include the milestone banner under every codebase page's title. It lives in one snippet file per project, so bumping it for a new milestone means editing one file:

    --8<-- "includes/2627-game/milestone.md"

    Snippet paths resolve from docs/, and files in docs/includes/ aren't built as pages.

  • End system pages with Known Issues, then Differs from the GDD (the project's Game Design Document) where the project has one. Start each item with a short bold summary that ends in a period, and link to the line in the source when one line is at fault.

  • Plain ASCII only in codebase pages. Write -> rather than an arrow character, and x rather than a times sign. Use TeX ($...$ inline, $$...$$ for a block) for any math or special symbol, and keep Mermaid labels ASCII.

Diagrams: Use Mermaid in a fenced block with the mermaid language. Use a class diagram for how classes connect, a state diagram for anything that changes state, and a flowchart for a pipeline. Prefer top-to-bottom layouts (direction TB, flowchart TB), because wide left-to-right diagrams shrink until their text is unreadable. The build doesn't check Mermaid, so preview the page with mkdocs serve and make sure the diagram draws.

Code blocks: Always specify the language identifier.

```csharp
// C# code
```
```gdscript
# GDScript
```
```bash
# shell
```

Use inline code for file paths (Assets/Scripts/), variable names (playerHealth), and menu items (File > Save).

Links: Use descriptive text: [Contributing Guide](index.md) not [click here](index.md). Use relative paths for internal links.

Admonitions:

!!! tip         helpful but optional
!!! info        neutral info
!!! warning     must-know before proceeding
!!! danger      serious, destructive
!!! example     worked example
!!! question    an exercise prompt
??? note        collapsible

Don't overuse them, as if every paragraph has one, none stand out.

Exercises: The programming onboarding guides use a consistent set of blocks for exercises. If you're writing a guide with exercises, reuse them so readers know what to expect:

Block Use it for !!! question "Predict: ..." Code or a scenario the reader predicts the outcome of before checking ??? success "Check your prediction" Right after a Predict: what happens, and why !!! example "Make: ..." A design or build exercise. Never include the answer. ??? tip "Hint 1", "Hint 2", "Hint 3" After a Make: a nudge question, then the concept with a docs link, then an approach in words (a little code is OK) ??? note "What a good answer includes" After the hints: criteria readers can check their own answer against, not a solution ??? info "New to this? ..." Background that experienced readers can skip !!! example "This week's game idea" One per onboarding guide. The only block that gets edited for a specific meeting.

Images: Store in docs/assets/images/. Always include alt text. Add an italic caption below.

![Description of image](../../assets/images/example.png)
*Caption here.*

Tags: Lowercase, hyphen-separated. Reuse existing tags before adding new ones.

programming, art, game-design, audio, general, unity, godot, unreal, pixel-art, 3d, animation, ui, tools, assets, project, game-jam, tutorial, reference, setup, beginner, intermediate, advanced

Difficulty ratings (tutorials):

Value Meaning beginner No prior knowledge needed intermediate Comfortable with basics advanced Significant experience expected

docs.title: Google Doc Template
docs.text:
Some things are easier to write in Google Docs, and some people just prefer it. You can put any Google Doc, Sheet, Slides deck, or Form straight onto the site, either as a whole page or inside a normal page.

The doc stays live. Edit it in Google Docs and the site shows the new version immediately, with no commit and no rebuild.

docs.title: Before You Embed
docs.text:
• The file lives in the SIGGD Shared Drive, not someone's personal Drive. Files in a personal Drive disappear when that person deletes them or leaves the club. Ask a lead if you don't have access to the shared drive.
  • Sharing is set to Anyone with the link (Viewer is enough). Without this, visitors see Google's "you need access" screen inside the frame.
  • You have the normal share link, the one the Share → Copy link button gives you.

Anyone with the link means anyone

The site is public, so treat an embedded file as public. Don't embed anything with personal information, and remember that a doc can be edited by anybody you've given edit access to, without review.

docs.title: A Whole Page That Is Just a Doc
docs.text:
Create a new .md file, give it a title, and point google_doc at your file. That's the entire page:

---
title: "Story Design Doc"
google_doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit?usp=sharing
---

You can write normal Markdown under the frontmatter too. It shows up above the embed, which is a good place for a sentence of context or a warning.

The right-hand table of contents is hidden automatically on these pages, since the site can't see the headings inside the file, and the embed takes the full width instead.

Then add the page to the nav: section of mkdocs.yml like any other page.

docs.title: A Doc Inside a Normal Page
docs.text:
Add { .google-doc } to an ordinary Markdown link:

[Story Design Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit){ .google-doc }

The link text becomes the frame's title for screen readers. If the embed ever breaks, this is still a working link to the doc.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
Embeds are as tall as most of your screen by default, and Slides keep a 16:9 shape. A cross-origin frame can't measure its own contents, so the document scrolls inside its frame rather than growing to fit.

To override the height, use any CSS length (a bare number means pixels):

[Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit){ .google-doc height="600" }

---
title: "Task Tracker"
google_doc: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/FILE_ID/edit
google_doc_height: 1200
---

docs.title: What Works
docs.text:
File type Paste this Notes Docs https://docs.google.com/document/d/FILE_ID/edit Sheets https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/FILE_ID/edit Embeds the whole spreadsheet, tabs included Slides https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/FILE_ID/edit Shown at 16:9 with Google's slide controls Forms https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/FORM_ID/viewform Use the live link from Send → link, not the editor link

Published links (File → Share → Publish to web) work too, and so does any embed URL you copy out of Google's own Embed dialog. Both are passed through as they are, so use them if you want Google's cleaner published view.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
• Site search can't see inside an embed. Searching the site won't find text that lives in the doc. If something needs to be findable, write it in Markdown instead.
  • The doc keeps its own look. A Google frame can't be restyled, so it stays white on our dark theme.
  • Google sets its own cookies inside the frame. Nothing else on this site does.
  • The "Open in Google Docs" button in the corner of every embed opens the real file in a new tab, which is where editing happens.
  • A bad link fails the build. If the URL isn't a Google file link, the pull request build says so, with the page name and the reason.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The frame says I need accessThe build failed on my pageThe embed is too short or too tall

Symptom: The embed shows a Google sign-in or "You need access" page.

Fix: Sharing isn't set to "Anyone with the link." Open the file, click Share, and change General access from "Restricted" to Anyone with the link.

Symptom: The PR build reports something like not a Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Forms link.

Fix: Use the link from the file's Share → Copy link button. A search-result link, a drive.google.com/file/... link, or a Forms editor link won't work.

Symptom: Lots of empty space, or a tiny scrolling window.

Fix: Set a height, as shown in Sizing.

docs.title: Add a Thing
docs.text:
A how-to is a recipe for one change someone makes often, like adding a gun or a sound. It assumes the reader already has the project open and knows what they want to build. Link to the system page for background instead of explaining the system again here.

One or two sentences on what the change involves (which assets, which classes), and a link to the system page. If the recipe builds an example, say what it is.

docs.title: 1. First Step
docs.text:
Numbered steps, each one action. Give exact paths and menu items:

  1. In Assets/YourSystem/, right-click and choose Create > Data > YourAsset.
  2. Set fieldName to the value it needs.

Code goes in a full, compilable example the reader can paste, following the C# Style Guide:

public class NewThing : BaseThing
{
    [SerializeField] private float strength = 1f;

    protected override void OnUse()
    {
        // ...
    }
}

After the code, list what the reader should copy from it into their own version.

docs.title: 3. Try It
docs.text: How to see the change working in the editor, and anything to undo before committing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
End with a checklist, a "Things to Watch For" list, or a Troubleshooting section (tabs work well for symptom and fix), whichever suits the recipe:

  • Units are right (seconds or milliseconds, degrees or radians).
  • New files are committed with their .meta files.

docs.title: Space Jam (26-27 Game)
docs.text:
Space Jam is a 2D boss rush where you, solo or with a friend, destroy evil planets. You float in zero gravity, build up speed with your jetpack and equipment, and damage each planet boss by ramming yourself or an asteroid into it. Speed = Damage = Good.

Engine Unity 6 (6000.3.21f1), 2D, Universal Render Pipeline Genre 2D side-view boss rush, physics-based, co-op Players 1 or 2, local Status In development. Milestone 1 shipped as v0.1.0. Source PurdueSIGGD/SIGGD-Game-2026

docs.title: The Game Loop
docs.text:
Each level is one boss fight against a planet. See the Game Design Document for more.

  1. Pick a loadout: a gun, a tool, and a passive.
  2. Fight the boss. Learn its attack patterns, dodge, and land hits by building speed.
  3. Win, earn a rank and a reward, and buy new equipment for the next fight.

What you can play at v0.1.0

One player fights the Factory Planet in a single phase, with the Pistol and the Bomb Thrower. Several things don't match the design yet: bullets do hurt the boss, the test asteroids hurt you instead of being pushable, robots are harmless, and nothing happens when either side dies. See the codebase overview.

docs.text:
1. Set up Unity Hub, Git, and the repo by following Getting Set Up.
  2. Open the project with Unity 6000.3.21f1.
  3. Open Assets/Scenes/MasterScene.unity. It's the only scene in the build.
  4. Press Play. Use the controls on the Overview page.

You should see the player, the Factory Planet spinning, and seven test asteroids drifting. The planet starts attacking as soon as the scene loads.

PlayerHealthTestScene and testplayermovement in Assets/Scenes/, and Test.unity in Assets/Equipment/LoadoutMenu/, are test scenes. They aren't in the build and may be out of date.

docs.title: Milestone 1 at a Glance
docs.text: System State at v0.1.0 Player Working. Movement, brake and relaunch, aiming, health with a short invincibility window after each hit. Co-op ghosts and revives work in code, but MasterScene only has one player. Damage and Health Working. One interface shared by the player, boss, robots, and asteroids. Weapons and Projectiles Working. One gun (the Pistol) with pooled bullets. Fire rate isn't limited yet, and spline bullets are a work in progress. Tools Working. The Bomb Thrower is the one tool. Loadout and Passives Partial. The loadout menu swaps guns. Tool swapping is stubbed out, and passives are stored but never applied. Boss Working. The Factory Planet picks weighted random attacks (scrap fan, lasers, robots). It has one phase and no death sequence. Asteroids Built but not placed. The full spawner, fragmenting, and pooling code exists, but no scene uses it yet. MasterScene uses seven simple test asteroids instead. Audio Working. FMOD one-shots and boss music, through a generated AudioEvents class. Shared Infrastructure Working. Singletons, an event bus, and an object pool. Only the singleton runs in the game. PrefabPool waits on the asteroid system, and the event bus isn't used yet.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Space Jam follows Unity's component model: each behavior is a small MonoBehaviour, and the numbers that tune it live in ScriptableObject assets. There's no central game manager yet. Systems find each other through prefab wiring, a few static entry points (ProjectileManager.Instance, PlayerRegistry, AudioManager), and the shared IDamageable interface.

flowchart TB
    INPUT["PlayerInputHandler<br/>(reads PlayerInput)"]
    INPUT --> MOVE["PlayerController<br/>movement and brake"]
    INPUT --> GUN["PrimaryGun"]
    INPUT --> TOOL["ToolUser + BombThrower"]

    BOSS["GenericBoss"] --> ATK["BossAttack assets"]

    GUN --> PM["ProjectileManager<br/>bullet pool"]
    TOOL --> PM
    ATK --> PM
    ATK --> LASER["Laser"]
    ATK --> ROBOT["Robot"]

    PM --> SHOTS["Bullet, Bomb"]
    MOVE --> RAM["Collisions faster than<br/>a speed threshold"]

    SHOTS -- "TakeDamage" --> DMG{{"IDamageable<br/>player, boss, robots, asteroids"}}
    LASER -- "TakeDamage" --> DMG
    RAM -- "boss and asteroids<br/>damage themselves" --> DMG

    REG[("PlayerRegistry")] -.-> ROBOT

Arrows show who calls or creates what. Robots read PlayerRegistry to chase the nearest player, but don't deal damage yet. AudioManager isn't shown. The gun, the boss and its attacks, and the player all call it to play sounds.

A few codebase rules:

  • Only PlayerInputHandler reads input. Everything else reads its properties (Move, IsBrakeHeld) or subscribes to its events (FirePressed, UseToolPressed). See Player.
  • Anything that can be hurt implements IDamageable. Attackers don't check what they hit. They build a DamageContext and call TakeDamage. The one exception is the MasterScene test asteroids, which check for the Player tag. See Damage and Health.
  • Collision damage is computed by the thing being hit. The boss and the asteroid system's asteroids each turn impact speed into damage to themselves. That's how "speed = damage" works in code.
  • Tuning numbers live in assets. Guns, bullets, boss attacks, player stats, and asteroids all read from ScriptableObjects. See the Tuning Guide.
  • Sounds go through AudioManager and AudioEvents. Do not type an FMOD path by hand. See Audio.

docs.text:
The 2D collision matrix (Project Settings > Physics 2D) lets every layer hit every other layer. Bullets, robots, and ghosts then exclude specific layers on their own colliders, and anything on an excluded layer passes through them.

Layer Index On it at v0.1.0 Skipped by Asteroid 8 The test asteroids Ghost players Player 9 The player prefab The player's own bullets Enemy 10 Nothing yet. Robots are still on Default. Boss bullets, robots Boss 11 The Factory Boss object Boss bullets, robots

Everything else, including robots, lasers, bullets, and bombs, is on Default.

Tags are listed as constants in PlayerSystem.Tags. Player is on the player prefab, and Finish marks whatever removes a ghost on contact (see Player).

docs.title: Code Conventions
docs.text:
The C# Style Guide covers naming and formatting, and the repo's .editorconfig mirrors it. Two project-specific notes:

  • Namespaces. Most player code is in PlayerSystem, and the shared extensions are in Extensions.EventBus and Extensions.Singleton. Everything else is in the global namespace for now.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms these pages use that are specific to Space Jam or to this codebase.

AOE bomb The boss's area-of-effect bomb attack (BossAttackBomb). Built, but not in the Factory Planet's attack pool. Brake and relaunch The player's brake: hold to stop dead, release while holding a direction to fly off at the saved speed. See Player. GDD The Game Design Document, the design team's source of truth for how the game should play. Ghost What a player becomes in co-op at 0 HP while a teammate is still alive. A ghost drifts toward the planet, and a living teammate can touch it to revive it. See Player. Invincibility window (i-frames) The short time after a hit when the player can't be hurt again. Set by IframeDuration. Kinematic A Rigidbody2D that physics doesn't move. The boss is kinematic, so rams don't push it. MasterScene Assets/Scenes/MasterScene.unity, the one scene in the build. Misc The old name for the tool slot. It still appears in the GDD and some code comments. Passive The third loadout slot: a stat change with no button. See Loadout and Passives. Phase A stage of a boss fight, set by the boss's health. Each phase can use different attack weights. See Boss. Pool A set of reusable objects that are switched off instead of destroyed. Bullets and asteroids are pooled. See Shared Infrastructure. Scrap fan The Factory Planet's basic bullet attack (BossAttackLinearFan). Telegraph A warning shown before an attack lands. The GDD asks for them, but none exist yet. Weight A number that sets how likely the boss is to pick an attack in a phase, stored in an AttackPercents asset. See Boss. World coordinates Positions in the scene itself, not relative to any object. Boss attack origins use them.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
1. Get the project open. If you haven't installed Unity and cloned the game, follow Getting Set Up first. It walks through GitHub Desktop and the right Unity version.
  2. Find the asset in Unity's Project window (bottom of the screen by default), using the path given in each section below.
  3. Click it. Its fields appear in the Inspector (right side). Each field below is listed by the name the Inspector shows.
  4. Change a value, then press Play in Assets/Scenes/MasterScene.unity to try it.
  5. Share the change. Either open a pull request with the changed .asset file (The PR Workflow shows how), or send the numbers to a programmer to put in.

Asset edits made during Play mode are kept

Changes to an object in the scene are thrown away when you stop playing, but changes to these assets are saved. That makes it easy to tune while playing, and just as easy to forget what you changed.

Changes in Unity may not save through Git

You may make changes to a scriptable object in Unity, but not see that in your Git tracking. To fix this, navigate to File → Save Project to write those changes to disk.

Units used below: distances are in units (Unity's world units), speeds in units per second, angles in degrees, and times in seconds unless a row says otherwise.

docs.title: Damage Numbers at v0.1.0
docs.text:
The player has 3 HP. Hits come from boss scrap bullets (1 each), lasers (1 per second while inside one), and the test asteroids (1 each). Robots deal no damage on contact. Getting caught in your own bomb's blast counts as a hit that does 0 damage but still slows you.

The boss has 100 HP. Hits come from rams and pushed objects moving faster than 5 units per second (10 damage per unit per second of speed), player bullets (5 each, with no fire-rate limit), and bombs (0 damage as shipped). The GDD says bullets shouldn't hurt the boss, so bullet damage to the boss is a known gap.

docs.title: Add a Boss Attack
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

Boss attacks are ScriptableObjects, so a new pattern is one class plus a few assets. Before you write code, check whether one of the four existing attack types can do it with different settings. More bullets, a different angle, or a new projectile needs only a new asset.

This recipe builds a ring: a burst of bullets in every direction at once, fired from the boss itself.

docs.title: 1. Write the Attack Class
docs.text:
Create Assets/GenericBoss/BossAttackRing.cs:

using Cysharp.Threading.Tasks;
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Fires one bullet in each of <c>bulletCount</c> evenly spaced directions from the boss.
/// </summary>
[CreateAssetMenu(fileName = "BossAttackRing", menuName = "Data/BossAttackRing")]
public class BossAttackRing : BossAttack
{
    [SerializeField] private ProjectileScriptableObject projectile;
    [SerializeField, Min(1)] private int bulletCount = 12;
    [SerializeField, Tooltip("Rotates the whole ring, in degrees.")] private float startAngle;
    [SerializeField] private LayerMask targetLayers;
    [SerializeField] private LayerMask ignoreLayers;

    public override UniTask Shoot(GameObject bossObject)
    {
        AudioManager.PlayOneShot(AudioEvents.Sound_Effects.Boss_1.Attacks.Boss_1_ShootScrap);

        for (int i = 0; i < bulletCount; i++)
        {
            float angle = startAngle + 360f * i / bulletCount;
            Vector2 direction = Quaternion.Euler(0f, 0f, angle) * Vector2.right;
            ProjectileManager.Instance.ShootProjectileTowardsDirection(
                projectile, bossObject.transform, direction, targetLayers, ignoreLayers);
        }

        return UniTask.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Things to copy from this into your own attack:

  • Shoot returns a task that finishes when the attack is done firing. This one fires everything at once, so it returns UniTask.CompletedTask right away. The boss waits for the task, then waits Cooldown seconds, then picks again.

  • An attack that fires over time should be async and wait between shots. Pass the boss's destroy token to each delay, so the attack stops if the boss is destroyed partway through. (The existing attacks don't, so they keep firing after the boss is gone.)

    public override async UniTask Shoot(GameObject bossObject)
{
    var token = bossObject.GetCancellationTokenOnDestroy();
    for (int i = 0; i < bulletCount; i++)
    {
        // fire one bullet here
        await UniTask.Delay(delayMilliseconds, cancellationToken: token);
    }
}

  • Fire from bossObject, not from fixed world coordinates. The existing attacks use world positions, so they break when the boss moves. Passing bossObject.transform as the fire point keeps the attack attached to the boss.

  • Put every number in a serialized field, so designers can make variants without touching code. The fields follow the C# Style Guide: [SerializeField] private, camelCase. (The older attack classes use [field: SerializeField] auto-properties instead.)

docs.title: 2. Make the Attack Asset
docs.text:
1. In Assets/GenericBoss/, right-click and choose Create > Data > BossAttackRing.
  2. Set Projectile to an existing boss bullet, such as Assets/Projectiles/Bullets/BossBasicBullet.asset.
  3. Set Ignore Layers to Boss and Enemy, so bullets spawned inside the boss don't hit it. (Target Layers has no effect at v0.1.0; see Weapons and Projectiles.)
  4. Set Cooldown, the seconds the boss rests after this attack. 2 is the default.

docs.title: 3. Give It a Weight
docs.text:
The boss reads its attacks through AttackPercents assets, which pair an attack with a weight for each phase.

  1. Right-click and choose Create > Data > AttackPercents.
  2. Set Attack to your new asset.
  3. Set ChanceWeights to one number per boss phase. The Factory Boss has one phase, so one entry, such as 1. An entry of 0 means "not in this phase".

One weight per phase, always

If a boss has three phases, every AttackPercents in its list needs three weights. A shorter array makes the boss read past the end of it when it reaches a later phase.

docs.title: 4. Add It to the Boss
docs.text: Open Assets/GenericBoss/Factory Boss Data.asset and add your AttackPercents to AttackPercentList.

docs.title: 5. Try It
docs.text: Press Play in MasterScene. To see your attack every time instead of about a quarter of the time, temporarily set the other attacks' weights to 0. When only one attack has weight, the boss is allowed to repeat it. Put the weights back before committing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Delays are in milliseconds (UniTask.Delay), and Cooldown is in seconds.
  • The attack plays a sound. If the right one doesn't exist yet, ask the audio team, then see Add a Sound Effect.
  • Every AttackPercents you touched has one weight per phase.
  • New .cs and .asset files are committed with their .meta files.

docs.title: Add a Gun
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

A gun is three assets and no code: a projectile (what comes out), a gun (how it fires), and a visual prefab (what the player holds). The quickest way to start is to copy the Pistol's three assets and change them. For how firing works, see Weapons and Projectiles.

docs.title: 1. Make the Projectile
docs.text:
Skip this step if an existing projectile works; several guns can share one.

  1. In Assets/Projectiles/Bullets/, duplicate PistolBullet.asset (Ctrl+D) and rename it, say SniperBullet.
  2. Set its fields. The Tuning Guide explains each one.
    • Damage, Lifetime (seconds), and Velocity (units per second).
    • Projectile Sprite. The bullet's collider takes this sprite's physics shape, so a long thin sprite gets a long thin hitbox.
    • Projectile Color and Projectile Scale to tint and size it without new art.
  3. Leave Spline Game Object empty. Spline bullets are a work in progress.

docs.title: 2. Make the Gun Visual
docs.text:
1. In Assets/Equipment/WeaponPrefabs/, duplicate Test_Pistol_Prefab.prefab and open it.
  2. Swap the sprite for your gun's art.
  3. Move the two child objects so they sit where they should:
    • Holdpoint goes where the hand grips the gun.
    • Firepoint goes at the muzzle. Bullets spawn here.

Make sure the root still has WeaponPrefabTransformHolder with both fields filled in. PrimaryGun reads it when the gun is equipped.

docs.title: 3. Make the Gun Asset
docs.text:
1. In Assets/Equipment/WeaponScriptableObjects/, right-click and choose Create > Scriptable Objects > PrimaryWeapon. (Or duplicate Pistol.asset. Don't duplicate Shotgun.asset, which is a projectile asset by mistake.)

  2. Fill it in:

    Field Set it to Projectile The projectile from step 1 Weapon Name The display name, shown by the loadout menu Num Bullets Bullets per shot. Use 1 for a single bullet. Spread Width of the bullet fan in degrees. With one bullet, the bullet lands at a random angle inside it. Offset Extra random angle per bullet, in degrees either way Recoil How hard each shot pushes the player backward Ammo Capacity Rounds in a full magazine Reload Time Seconds to refill from empty. Refilling is continuous. Weapon Visual Prefab The prefab from step 2 Weapon Visual Rotation Offset Degrees to rotate the visual if it points the wrong way Fire Speed Anything. It's unused at v0.1.0, since fire rate isn't limited yet.

docs.title: 4. Try It
docs.text:
1. Open Assets/Player/Player.prefab, select WeaponHolder, and drag your gun asset into Primary Gun > Weapon.
  2. Press Play in MasterScene and shoot.
  3. Undo the prefab change before you commit, unless your gun should be the new default. To offer it as a choice instead, give it a button in the loadout menu.

docs.title: Things to Watch For
docs.text:
• Multi-bullet guns. Bullets collide with each other at v0.1.0, so a shotgun's pellets that spawn overlapping cancel each other out at the muzzle. See Known Issues.
  • Recoil and the speed cap. The player's speed is clamped to Max Velocity every physics step, so at top speed recoil can turn you or slow you down, but not add lasting speed.
  • Commit the .meta files. Every new asset has a matching .meta file, and Unity loses references without it.

docs.title: Add a Sound Effect
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

The audio team adds the event in FMOD Studio and builds the banks. A programmer then refreshes the generated AudioEvents class and adds one line of code. For how the pipeline works, see Audio.

docs.title: Audio Team: Add and Build the Event
docs.text:
1. Open FMODProject/SpaceJam_FMOD/SpaceJam_FMOD.fspro in FMOD Studio 2.03. The game runs FMOD for Unity 2.03.14, and FMOD only loads banks built by the same 2.03 version line.
  2. Create the event in the folder that matches where it's used, such as Sound Effects/Player/Gun/. The folder path becomes the C# name, so Sound Effects/Player/Gun/Sniper_Shoot becomes AudioEvents.Sound_Effects.Player.Gun.Sniper_Shoot.
  3. Assign the event to a bank (usually Sound Effects or Music).
  4. File > Build. The project is set to write banks to FMOD/ at the repo root, which updates the files in FMOD/Desktop/.
  5. Commit the changed FMODProject/ files and the rebuilt .bank files together, and say in the PR which event is new and where it should play.

docs.title: Programmer: Refresh the Event List
docs.text:
1. Pull the audio team's change and open Unity. FMOD for Unity notices the new banks on its own.
  2. Choose Tools > Audio > Refresh Audio Events.
  3. The Console should say Wrote N audio events to Assets/Audio/AudioEvents.cs. If it says they're already up to date, Unity hasn't picked up the new banks yet. Check that the pull included the .bank files, then refresh again.

docs.title: Programmer: Play It
docs.text:
Call AudioManager.PlayOneShot with the new field wherever the sound should happen:

AudioManager.PlayOneShot(AudioEvents.Sound_Effects.Player.Gun.Sniper_Shoot);

AudioManager's methods are static, so there's nothing to look up or assign first. If the audio team made the event 3D, pass a position so it plays from the right place:

AudioManager.PlayOneShot(AudioEvents.Sound_Effects.Boss_1.Boss_1_Hurt, transform.position);

Commit the regenerated AudioEvents.cs in the same PR as the code that uses it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The field doesn't existNo sound playsMusic plays twice

Symptom: AudioEvents has no field for the event, so the code doesn't compile.

Fix: Refresh the event list (above). If it's still missing, the event isn't in a bank, or the banks weren't rebuilt after it was added. Ask the audio team to check its bank assignment and build again.

Symptom: The code runs, but you hear nothing.

Fix: Check the Console for an [FMOD] Event not found warning, or an EventNotFoundException for music. Either one means the generated class is newer than the banks you have, so pull the latest banks. Then check that MasterScene's Main Camera still has its StudioListener.

Symptom: Starting a second music track doesn't stop the first.

Fix: That's a known bug in AudioManager.PlayTrack at v0.1.0, not your event.

docs.title: Add a Tool
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

A tool is a component that extends Tool and implements OnUse(). The base class handles the cooldown, and ToolUser handles input, so your class only says what the tool does. For background, see Tools.

This recipe builds the GDD's Shockwave Shield: an instant blast centered on the player that shoves everything nearby away and leaves the player in place.

Pick the right base class

  • Tools that throw something (bombs, grapples, portals) extend ProjectileTool and come with their own ToolProjectile subclass. Copy BombThrower and Bomb.
  • Everything else extends Tool directly, like this recipe.

docs.title: 1. Write the Tool Class
docs.text:
Create Assets/Equipment/Tools/Scripts/Tools/ShockwaveShield.cs:

using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Pushes every dynamic body near the player away from them. The player isn't moved.
/// </summary>
public class ShockwaveShield : Tool
{
    [SerializeField, Min(0f)] private float radius = 3f;
    [SerializeField] private float impulse = 15f;

    private readonly HashSet<Rigidbody2D> pushed = new HashSet<Rigidbody2D>();

    protected override void OnUse()
    {
        // This component sits on WeaponHolder, out at the player's hand, so center the
        // blast on the player's body instead of on this object.
        Rigidbody2D self = GetComponentInParent<Rigidbody2D>();
        Vector2 origin = self != null ? self.worldCenterOfMass : (Vector2)transform.position;
        pushed.Clear();

        foreach (Collider2D hit in Physics2D.OverlapCircleAll(origin, radius))
        {
            Rigidbody2D body = hit.attachedRigidbody;
            if (body == null || body == self || body.bodyType != RigidbodyType2D.Dynamic)
            {
                continue;
            }

            // A body with several colliders shows up once per collider.
            if (!pushed.Add(body))
            {
                continue;
            }

            Vector2 away = (body.worldCenterOfMass - origin).normalized;
            body.AddForce(away * impulse, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        }
    }
}

What this relies on from Tool:

  • Use() runs OnUse() only when the cooldown is ready. You don't check cooldowns yourself. The cooldown comes from the tool's ToolData asset.
  • UseAlt() is the second button. It runs when the player holds E or the gamepad's north button for 0.4 s, because the input action uses a Hold interaction. Override it if your tool has an alternate action, like detonating a remote bomb. Unlike Use(), it has no cooldown.

docs.title: 2. Make the Tool's Data
docs.text:
1. In Assets/Equipment/Tools/Scriptable Objects/Tools/, right-click and choose Create > Scriptable Objects > ToolData. Name it ShockwaveShieldData.
  2. In the Inspector, set Cooldown (in seconds) and Tool Name.

docs.title: 3. Put It on the Player
docs.text:
1. Open Assets/Player/Player.prefab and select WeaponHolder. It already has PrimaryGun, BombThrower, and ToolUser.
  2. Add your ShockwaveShield component and drag ShockwaveShieldData into its Data field.
  3. In ToolUser, set Secondary Tool to your new component. ToolUser only uses that one tool, so BombThrower can stay on the object.

docs.title: 4. Try It
docs.text:
Press Play in MasterScene and right-click next to one of the test asteroids. Do it in the first few seconds, because the test asteroids destroy themselves about 7 seconds in, or as soon as they touch anything.

Before committing, decide whether your tool replaces the Bomb Thrower as the default. If it doesn't, set Secondary Tool back to BombThrower and keep your component on the prefab so it's ready for the loadout menu. At v0.1.0 the menu can't switch tools yet.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Tuning numbers are serialized fields or live in a data asset, not hard-coded. If designers will tune the tool a lot, move them into a ToolData subclass, the way BombData extends ToolProjectileData.
  • The tool plays a sound, or there's a request in to the audio team. See Add a Sound Effect.
  • New .cs and .asset files are committed with their .meta files.

docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

Asteroids are Space Jam's ammunition. In the GDD, players push them into the boss. The asteroid system spawns asteroids off-screen and drifts them into view, damages them by impact speed, and splits them into fragments that carry the parent's momentum. Everything is pooled.

Built, but not in the game yet

No scene or prefab uses AsteroidSpawner or AsteroidController at v0.1.0, and there are no AsteroidData assets yet. MasterScene uses seven simpler test asteroids instead.

  • Folder: Assets/Asteroids/
  • Namespace: global
  • Tuning: asteroids

docs.title: Life of an Asteroid
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pooled
    Pooled --> Drifting : PrefabPool.Get() + Initialize()
    Drifting --> Drifting : hit slower than the threshold (no damage)
    Drifting --> Breaking : health reaches 0
    Breaking --> Pooled : explosion + fragments spawned, Died raised
    Drifting --> Pooled : leaves an AsteroidDespawnZone

Damage is applied in OnCollisionEnter2D, but the asteroid only breaks on its next Update, so new fragments never spawn in the middle of a physics callback.

docs.title: Spawning
docs.text:
Every Period seconds, AsteroidSpawner:

  1. Picks a random target point inside the target area: the camera's view or the spawner's BoxCollider2D, shrunk by TargetInset on every side.
  2. Picks a direction of travel within Spread degrees of CenterAngle. Here 0 is right and 90 is up.
  3. Backs up from the target along that direction until it's outside the camera view plus OffscreenMargin, and at least MinTravelDistance away. That's the spawn point.
  4. Launches the asteroid toward the target at a speed chosen so linear damping brings it to rest near the target point.

Unity's 2D physics scales velocity by \(1 / (1 + c\,\Delta t)\) every physics step, where \(c\) is the linear damping and \(\Delta t\) is the fixed timestep. Treated as smooth exponential decay, that's a decay rate of \(k = \ln(1 + c\,\Delta t) / \Delta t\), and an object decaying at rate \(k\) from speed \(v_0\) travels \(v_0 / k\) before stopping. Setting that equal to the distance \(d\) gives the launch speed ComputeLaunchSpeed returns:

\[ v_0 = d \cdot \frac{\ln(1 + c\,\Delta t)}{\Delta t} \]

Because the physics runs in discrete steps, the asteroid stops slightly short: about 1% short at the default damping of 1, and about 5% short at a damping of 5.

docs.title: Impact Damage
docs.text: Any collision faster than speedDamageThreshold damages the asteroid by the impact speed times damageMultiplier. It only damages itself; the boss works out its own damage from the same collision. See Damage and Health.

docs.title: Splitting
docs.text:
When an asteroid breaks, it spawns its ExplosionPrefab and DebrisCount fragments using FragmentPrefab and FragmentData. Fragments can split again if their own data has a DebrisCount above 0. AsteroidData.OnValidate reports an error if the chain of FragmentData loops back on itself.

Each of the \(n\) fragments gets mass \(m_f = m / n\) and scale \(s / \sqrt{n}\), so the fragments' total area matches the parent's. They spawn spread evenly around the parent's center. Each one gets an outward impulse \(\vec{J}_i\) of about ExplosionImpulse, randomized by ImpulseVariationPercentage. The average impulse is then subtracted from all of them so they sum to exactly zero. Each fragment's velocity is

\[ \vec{v}_i = \vec{v}_{\text{parent}} + \frac{\vec{J}_i}{m_f} \]

and because the impulses cancel, total momentum is unchanged:

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_f\,\vec{v}_i = m\,\vec{v}_{\text{parent}} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \vec{J}_i = m\,\vec{v}_{\text{parent}} \]

Fragments also inherit the parent's spin and damping. Freshly spawned fragments overlap and would immediately damage each other, so each pair ignores collisions with each other until they're siblingClearance apart.

docs.title: The Explosion Effect
docs.text: ExplosionEffect is a pooled sprite that grows to endScaleMultiplier times its starting size and fades out along alphaCurve over duration seconds. It moves at the dead asteroid's velocity. The default curve stays fully opaque for the first 30% of the effect, so the fragments underneath are hidden until the flash fades.

docs.title: The Test Asteroids in MasterScene
docs.text: The seven asteroids in MasterScene come from Assets/Player/PlayerHealthTesting/Asteroid.prefab, which was built to test player health. Each one drifts in a random direction at 3 units/s and is destroyed 20 units from where it started, so about 7 seconds after the scene starts. Any collision destroys it, and if it hits a player, it deals that player 1 damage. Touching one hurts you instead of pushing it, so you can't steer them into the boss yet. Spawner.cs in the same folder spawns them on a timer in PlayerHealthTestScene.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

All game audio goes through FMOD. The audio team builds events in FMOD Studio, and code plays them with one line, AudioManager.PlayOneShot(AudioEvents.<path>). AudioEvents is a generated C# class with one field per FMOD event, so a typo in an event name is a compile error instead of a silent missing sound.

  • Folder: Assets/Audio/
  • Namespace: global

docs.title: From FMOD Studio to Code
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["FMOD Studio project<br/>FMODProject/SpaceJam_FMOD"] -- "Build (audio team)" --> B["Banks<br/>FMOD/Desktop/*.bank"]
    B -- "read by FMOD for Unity" --> C["Unity editor"]
    C -- "Tools > Audio > Refresh Audio Events" --> D["Assets/Audio/AudioEvents.cs"]
    D --> E["AudioManager.PlayOneShot(...)"]
  1. The audio team edits FMODProject/SpaceJam_FMOD/SpaceJam_FMOD.fspro in FMOD Studio and builds it.
  2. The built banks (Master, Master.strings, Music, Sound Effects, Voice Lines) are committed under FMOD/Desktop/ at the repo root. FMOD for Unity is set to read them from there (FMOD > Edit Settings, bank source FMOD), and copies them into StreamingAssets/FMODBanks when you build the game.
  3. A programmer runs Tools > Audio > Refresh Audio Events in Unity, which rewrites AudioEvents.cs from the banks.
  4. Code references the new field.

docs.title: The Generated AudioEvents Class
docs.text:
The generator turns each event path into nested static classes, one per FMOD folder, ending in a static readonly EventReference. For example, event:/Sound Effects/Player/Misc/Player_Hurt becomes:

AudioEvents.Sound_Effects.Player.Misc.Player_Hurt

To make every path a legal C# name, the generator:

  • replaces anything that isn't a letter, digit, or underscore with _ (so Sound Effects becomes Sound_Effects),
  • adds a leading _ to names that start with a digit or are C# keywords,
  • adds _Event to an event whose name matches a sibling folder, and _2, _3, and so on to duplicates.

Each field stores the event's GUID, which is what FMOD uses in a build. The readable path is only compiled into the editor, inside #if UNITY_EDITOR.

Each refresh rewrites the whole file, so hand edits don't survive.

• Music tracks stack. PlayTrack creates the new instance in a local variable and never stores it in currentMusicTrack. The check that stops the previous track never finds one, so starting a second track plays both. No track is ever released either.

docs.title: Boss
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

A boss is one GenericBoss component driven by a BossData asset. The boss loops forever: pick a weighted random attack for the current phase, wait for it to finish firing, wait out its cooldown, repeat. Attacks are ScriptableObject assets, so a new boss is mostly a new set of assets. The Factory Planet is the only boss at v0.1.0.

  • Folders: Assets/GenericBoss/ (logic and the Factory Planet's attack assets), Assets/Boss/Factory Planet/ (the Factory Boss prefab and art)
  • Namespace: global
  • Tuning: boss

docs.title: How It's Put Together
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction TB
    class GenericBoss {
        +int CurrentPhase
        +float CurrentHealth
        +UnityEvent OnBossTakeDamage
        +UnityEvent OnBossDeath
        +TakeDamage(context)
    }
    class BossData {
        <<ScriptableObject>>
        +int[] PhaseHealthBoundaries
        +AttackPercents[] AttackPercentList
        +EventReference BossSoundTrack
    }
    class AttackPercents {
        <<ScriptableObject>>
        +uint[] ChanceWeights
        +BossAttack Attack
    }
    class BossAttack {
        <<abstract ScriptableObject>>
        +float Cooldown
        +Shoot(bossObject)* UniTask
    }
    class BossAttackLinearFan
    class BossAttackBomb
    class BossAttackLaser
    class BossAttackRobotSpawn
    class Laser
    class Robot
    class IDamageable {
        <<interface>>
    }
    GenericBoss --> BossData
    BossData --> AttackPercents : one per attack
    AttackPercents --> BossAttack
    BossAttack <|-- BossAttackLinearFan
    BossAttack <|-- BossAttackBomb
    BossAttack <|-- BossAttackLaser
    BossAttack <|-- BossAttackRobotSpawn
    BossAttackLaser ..> Laser : spawns 2
    BossAttackRobotSpawn ..> Robot : spawns
    BossAttackLinearFan ..> ProjectileManager
    BossAttackBomb ..> ProjectileManager
    GenericBoss ..|> IDamageable
    Robot ..|> IDamageable

Three layers of assets describe a boss:

  1. BossData, one per boss: health per phase, collision damage settings, music, and the list of attacks.
  2. AttackPercents, one per attack in that list: which BossAttack to use, and a weight for each phase.
  3. BossAttack subclasses, one per attack variant: the pattern (projectile, count, angles, timing).

The same BossAttack asset can appear in several bosses' lists with different weights.

docs.title: Names for the Same Attack
docs.text:
Each Factory Planet attack goes by several names, depending on whether you're reading the GDD, the code, or the Project window:

In the GDD and these docs Class Attack asset Weight asset Scrap fan BossAttackLinearFan BossAtkLinearFan.asset BasicAttack.asset (BasicPercent.asset is an unused duplicate) Lasers BossAttackLaser BossAttackLaser.asset LaserAttack.asset Robot spawn BossAttackRobotSpawn BossAttackRobotSpawn.asset RobotSpawn.asset AOE bomb (not in use) BossAttackBomb BossAttackBomb.asset BombPercent.asset (not in any list)

docs.title: The Attack Loop
docs.text:
GenericBoss.Start fills health, starts the boss music with AudioManager.PlayTrack, and starts AttackLoop, an async UniTask method.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Choosing
    Choosing --> Attacking : weighted random pick
    Attacking --> Cooldown : Shoot() task completes
    Cooldown --> Choosing : attack.Cooldown seconds pass
    Choosing --> Stopped : every weight is 0 (logs an error)
    Choosing --> Stopped : boss dead or destroyed
    Stopped --> [*]

Shoot() returns a task that completes once the attack has finished firing. Projectiles, lasers, and robots it created keep going after that.

The loop holds a cancellation token tied to the boss object, so destroying the boss stops the loop from waiting on the current attack or cooldown. Shoot() itself doesn't receive that token, though. An attack that awaits its own delays, like the scrap fan, keeps firing to the end even after the boss is gone.

docs.title: Picking an Attack
docs.text:
Each AttackPercents has a ChanceWeights array with one entry per phase. In phase p, an attack's chance is its ChanceWeights[p] divided by the sum of every attack's weight for p. Two extra rules:

  • The attack used last time is excluded, so the boss doesn't repeat itself. If it's the only attack with weight above 0, it's allowed to repeat.
  • A weight of 0 removes an attack from that phase.

For example, ignoring the no-repeat rule, weights of 3, 1, and 0 in phase 1 make the first attack fire 75% of the time and the third never fire.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
PhaseHealthBoundaries lists the health at which each phase starts, highest first. The first entry is also the boss's max health. With [100, 60, 25]:

Health Phase (CurrentPhase) 100 down to 60 0 Below 60 down to 25 1 Below 25 2

The phase only moves forward, and a single big hit can skip a phase. Every AttackPercents in the boss's list needs a ChanceWeights entry for every phase, or picking an attack in a later phase reads past the end of the array.

docs.title: Taking Damage
docs.text: GenericBoss implements IDamageable. Anything that collides with it faster than SpeedDamageThreshold (relative speed, in units per second) damages it for speed x DamageMultiplier. That's how rams and pushed asteroids hurt the boss. Player bullets and bombs hurt it through TakeDamage too. At 0 health, IsAlive turns false and OnBossDeath is raised. The attack loop checks IsAlive between attacks, so the boss finishes its current attack and cooldown before it stops.

docs.title: The Attack Types
docs.text:
All positions are world coordinates, not offsets from the boss. The bossObject parameter that Shoot receives isn't used yet. The attacks use different angle conventions, listed in the Angles column.

Attack What it does Angles BossAttackLinearFan Fires ProjectileCount bullets one at a time from Origin, Delay ms apart. Each shot turns by AngleOffset degrees and moves the origin HOffset units along x. Plays the scrap sound per shot. 0 = up, positive turns clockwise BossAttackBomb Fires ProjectileCount projectiles from Origin, Delay ms apart, aimed where the player will be in one second (position plus velocity). Aimed, no angle field BossAttackLaser Spawns two Laser beams from Origin, at LeftAngle and RightAngle, each Length long. They hurt every IDamageable inside them for Damage once per second and vanish after Lifetime seconds. Finishes instantly. 0 = right, positive turns counterclockwise BossAttackRobotSpawn Spawns ProjectileCount robots from Origin, Delay ms apart, launched in a fan like LinearFan. Each robot dashes at the nearest player every 3 seconds. 0 = up, positive turns clockwise

Delay is in milliseconds and Cooldown is in seconds.

docs.title: How a Laser Hits
docs.text: A Laser is a trigger collider with no Rigidbody2D. OnTriggerEnter2D adds whatever enters it to a list, and OnTriggerExit2D removes it. A timer then damages everything in the list once per second. The timer starts at zero when the laser spawns, so nothing takes damage during the beam's first second.

The AOE bomb exists but isn't in the list. Cooldown 2 s after every attack (the default; no asset overrides it) Music Boss_1_Music

The planet spins at 5 degrees per second through PlanetRotation. Its Rigidbody2D is kinematic, so collisions don't move it.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
• Nothing happens when the boss dies. The attack loop stops, but OnBossDeath has no listeners, so the planet sits idle. There's no victory sequence or return to a menu.
  • The laser breaks on non-damageable objects. Laser adds whatever GetComponent<IDamageable>() returns to its list, including null for non-damageable colliders such as the test asteroids. The damage tick then throws a NullReferenceException on that entry, and nothing after it in the list takes damage.
  • Lasers last 500 seconds. The Factory Planet's laser asset has Lifetime set to 500. Laser counts it in seconds, so every laser attack leaves two beams on screen for over eight minutes. The value may have been meant as milliseconds.
  • Robots don't hurt the player. Robot stores a damage value but never applies it. Touching one does nothing.
  • Robots are on the Default layer, not Enemy. Layer masks that mention Enemy don't affect them.
  • Attacks ignore the boss's position. Every origin is a world coordinate. The Factory Boss object sits at x = 28.8, but the scrap fan and robots fire from (1, 1).
  • BossAttackBomb targets one player. It finds a target with FindAnyObjectByType<Player>() instead of PlayerRegistry. Its projectile (BossBomb) is also marked explosive, which Bullet doesn't support yet.
  • The scrap fan runs for 50 seconds. The Factory Planet's fan fires 100 shots 500 ms apart, and the boss can't start another attack until it finishes.
  • Robot colliders may be empty in builds. Robots build their collider from a projectile asset, the same way bullets do. See Weapons and Projectiles.
  • Leftover code and assets. BasicPercent.asset duplicates BasicAttack.asset, BombPercent.asset isn't in any boss's list, and BossAttack declares four private fields its subclasses never use.
  • The boss can die more than once, and ResetHealth throws. See Damage and Health.

docs.title: Differs from the GDD
docs.text:
The GDD's Factory Planet section describes more than v0.1.0 builds:

  • Two phases. The code has one. The GDD's phase 2 adds accelerating robots, an aimed laser, and a splitting bomb.
  • Weights. The GDD's phase 1 is scrap (high), robots (medium), bomb (medium), lasers (low). The code has scrap, lasers, and robots at equal weight, and no bomb.
  • Laser sway and telegraphs. The GDD's lasers sway, and attacks get warning indicators. Neither exists yet.
  • Damage visuals. The GDD shows boss health through tint and cracks instead of a bar. There's no health display yet.
  • Ranking and asteroid hostility aren't implemented. Ranking grades the players at the end of a fight, and asteroid hostility is the boss turning idle asteroids against the player.

docs.title: Damage and Health
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

Everything that can be hurt implements one interface, IDamageable. Anything that deals damage builds a DamageContext and calls TakeDamage on whatever it hit, without knowing whether that's a player, the boss, a robot, or an asteroid. Each damageable object decides for itself what a hit means.

  • Folder: Assets/Damage/
  • Namespace: global

docs.title: How It's Put Together
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction TB
    class IDamageable {
        <<interface>>
        +float CurrentHealth
        +float MaxHealth
        +bool IsAlive
        +TakeDamage(DamageContext context)
        +ResetHealth()
    }
    class DamageContext {
        <<struct>>
        +float DamageAmount
        +GameObject Attacker
        +GameObject Victim
    }
    IDamageable ..> DamageContext
    PlayerHealth ..|> IDamageable
    GenericBoss ..|> IDamageable
    Robot ..|> IDamageable
    AsteroidController ..|> IDamageable

docs.title: Who Takes Damage
docs.text: Implementer What a hit does PlayerHealth Subtracts damage, then starts a short invincibility window and ignores hits during it. At 0 the player dies or becomes a ghost. GenericBoss Subtracts damage, raises OnBossTakeDamage, and moves to a later phase if health crossed a boundary. At 0 it raises OnBossDeath. Robot Subtracts damage. At 0 it raises OnRobotDeath and destroys itself. AsteroidController Subtracts damage. At 0 it explodes into fragments on its next Update.

docs.title: Who Deals Damage
docs.text:
Source How it hits Damage Bullet OnTriggerEnter2D with anything that has an IDamageable The projectile asset's Damage Laser Every IDamageable inside its trigger, once per second The laser attack's Damage Bomb Every living IDamageable in its blast radius BombData.blastDamage Test Asteroid OnCollisionEnter2D with the player 1 A collision with the boss or an asteroid The boss or asteroid damages itself Impact speed x a multiplier

That last row is how the "speed = damage" pillar works. When something hits the boss faster than SpeedDamageThreshold, GenericBoss damages itself:

\[ \text{damage} = |\vec{v}_{\text{relative}}| \times \text{DamageMultiplier} \]

AsteroidController uses the same formula with its own fields. Rams and pushed asteroids both work through this path. Because the boss computes its own collision damage, the player and the asteroid that hits it need no damage-dealing code.

docs.title: IDamageable
docs.text:
IDamageable.cs: interface

Member Type Description CurrentHealth float (get) Health right now. MaxHealth float (get) Full health. IsAlive bool (get) Whether the object can still take hits. TakeDamage(DamageContext) method Apply a hit. ResetHealth() method Return to full health, for restarting a fight.

docs.title: DamageContext
docs.text:
IDamageable.cs: struct

Field Type Description DamageAmount float How much health to remove. Attacker GameObject The object that caused the hit, such as a bullet, laser, or bomb. Victim GameObject The object that was hit.

Build one with the constructor or with an object initializer. Both styles appear in the code:

// Constructor (Bullet.cs)
damageable.TakeDamage(new DamageContext(damage, gameObject, other.gameObject));

// Object initializer (GenericBoss.cs)
TakeDamage(new DamageContext
{
    DamageAmount = damageAmount,
    Attacker = collision.gameObject,
    Victim = gameObject
});

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
• GenericBoss.ResetHealth() throws. It's still NotImplementedException, so anything that resets the fight through IDamageable crashes on the boss.
  • Laser doesn't null-check. It adds whatever GetComponent<IDamageable>() returns, including null, so a non-damageable object inside a beam makes its damage tick throw. See Boss.
  • No teams. Nothing in DamageContext says who's on which side. Bullets avoid friendly fire through collision layers only. Lasers and bombs hurt every IDamageable they touch, and GenericBoss has a TODO to check whether the attacker is allowed to hurt it.
  • A 0-damage hit still counts. PlayerHealth treats any TakeDamage call as a hit, even for 0 damage: it plays the hurt sound, slows the player, and starts the invincibility window. GenericBoss raises OnBossTakeDamage for it too.
  • The boss can "die" more than once. GenericBoss.TakeDamage doesn't return early when already dead, so every hit after the killing blow raises OnBossDeath again.
  • Integer damage on projectiles. ProjectileScriptableObject.Damage is an int while DamageAmount is a float, so bullets can't deal fractional damage.

docs.title: Differs from the GDD
docs.text: • Bullets hurt the boss. The GDD says bullets only clear projectiles and break asteroids. At v0.1.0, a player bullet deals its Damage to anything damageable, including the boss.

docs.title: Shared Infrastructure
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

These pieces know nothing about Space Jam. They're general patterns the systems build on: singleton base classes, a type-safe event bus, and an object pool. At v0.1.0, only Singleton<T> runs in the game, through ProjectileManager. PrefabPool is used by the asteroid system, which isn't in a scene yet. The event bus is ready but unused.

  • Folders: Assets/Extensions/, Assets/Asteroids/Scripts/PrefabPool.cs
  • Namespaces: Extensions.Singleton, Extensions.EventBus, and global for PrefabPool

docs.title: Singletons
docs.text:
Three base classes give a class one global instance reachable through T.Instance. They differ in what they wrap and what happens when no instance exists yet.

classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Singleton~T~ {
        <<MonoBehaviour>>
        +T Instance$
    }
    class PersistentSingleton~T~ {
        <<MonoBehaviour>>
        +T Instance$
        +T Current$
        +bool HasInstance$
        +bool UnparentOnAwake
    }
    class LazySingleton~T~ {
        +T Instance$
    }
    Singleton~T~ <|-- ProjectileManager
Singleton<T> PersistentSingleton<T> LazySingleton<T> Wraps A MonoBehaviour placed in the scene A MonoBehaviour, placed or not A plain C# class with a parameterless constructor If none exists Instance searches the scene (inactive objects included), logs a warning, and returns null Instance searches the scene, then creates a GameObject named <T>AutoCreated Created on first access Survives scene loads Yes, DontDestroyOnLoad Yes, DontDestroyOnLoad Not a scene object A second copy Destroyed in Awake, with a warning Destroyed in Awake Not prevented: T needs a public parameterless constructor, so new T() anywhere makes another Used by at v0.1.0 ProjectileManager Nothing Nothing

ProjectileManager inherits Singleton<T> with itself as T, and calls the base Awake from its own:

public class ProjectileManager : Singleton<ProjectileManager>
{
    protected override void Awake()
    {
        base.Awake();
        // your setup
    }
}

PersistentSingleton<T> also has UnparentOnAwake (on by default). It detaches the object from its parent before marking it DontDestroyOnLoad, because Unity only keeps root objects across scene loads.

docs.title: EventBus
docs.text:
EventBus<T> lets one system announce something without knowing who's listening. Each event type gets its own static bus, so listeners for one event never see another.

  1. Declare an event as a struct implementing IEvent, carrying whatever data listeners need.
  2. Listeners wrap a handler in an EventBinding<T> and register it.
  3. Anyone raises the event, and every registered binding runs its OnEvent and then its OnEventNoArgs.
using Extensions.EventBus;
using UnityEngine;

public struct BossPhaseChanged : IEvent
{
    public int Phase;
}

public class PhaseMusic : MonoBehaviour
{
    EventBinding<BossPhaseChanged> binding;

    void OnEnable()
    {
        binding = new EventBinding<BossPhaseChanged>(OnPhaseChanged);
        EventBus<BossPhaseChanged>.Register(binding);
    }

    void OnDisable() => EventBus<BossPhaseChanged>.Deregister(binding);

    void OnPhaseChanged(BossPhaseChanged e) => Debug.Log($"Phase {e.Phase}");
}

// Somewhere else, when the phase changes:
EventBus<BossPhaseChanged>.Raise(new BossPhaseChanged { Phase = 1 });

BossPhaseChanged is an example; no game events exist yet. The only IEvent in the code is an empty TestEvent.

Type Members EventBus<T> (static class, T : IEvent) Register(EventBinding<T>), Deregister(EventBinding<T>), Raise(T), Clear() EventBinding<T> Constructors taking Action<T> or Action (for handlers that don't need the data); Add and Remove for either kind; public OnEvent and OnEventNoArgs delegates IEvent Marker interface, no members EventBusEditorUtils (editor only) Clears every bus when you exit Play mode, so stale bindings don't leak into the next run

docs.title: PrefabPool
docs.text:
PrefabPool reuses instances of any prefab instead of destroying and instantiating them. Call Get where you'd call Instantiate, and Release where you'd call Destroy.

AsteroidController asteroid = PrefabPool.Get(asteroidPrefab, spawnPosition, Quaternion.identity);
asteroid.Initialize(velocity, damping);   // a reused instance keeps its old state, so reset it

// later, instead of Destroy(asteroid.gameObject):
PrefabPool.Release(asteroid.gameObject);
Member Description Get<T>(T prefab, Vector3 position, Quaternion rotation) (T : Component) Returns an active instance of prefab at that pose, reusing a released one when possible. Release(GameObject instance) Deactivates the instance for reuse. An object that didn't come from Get is destroyed instead. Releasing the same object twice throws in the editor.

There's one pool per prefab, created on first use. Each pool keeps up to 128 released instances, and any released past that are destroyed. Instances live under a PrefabPoolRoot object in the scene. When the scene unloads and takes that root with it, the next Get starts fresh pools.

docs.title: Two Pools in One Codebase
docs.text: Bullets don't use PrefabPool. ProjectileManager owns its own ObjectPool<GameObject> for the one bullet prefab (see Weapons and Projectiles). PrefabPool works for any prefab.

docs.title: Bootstrapper
docs.text: Bootstrapper.cs is an empty MonoBehaviour in no scene. Its comment says it will initialize game systems.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
• Bullets won't survive a scene reload. ProjectileManager is DontDestroyOnLoad, but the bullets in its pool are root objects in the scene. Reloading the scene destroys the bullets while the pool still holds them, so the next shot hands out a destroyed object.
  • Changing bindings during Raise throws. EventBus<T>.Raise loops over a HashSet, so registering or deregistering a binding for the same event from inside a handler throws InvalidOperationException.

Each button holds one choice, and a LoadoutTarget on the menu panel forwards clicks to that player's components. docs.title: The Menu
docs.text:
1. A LoadoutTarget sits on the menu panel and holds references to one player's PrimaryGun, Tool, and PassiveHolder.
  2. Each choice is its own button, a child of that panel. Gun and passive buttons hold an asset (a PrimaryWeapon or a Passive). A tool button holds a component: a reference to a Tool on that specific player, because tools are MonoBehaviours, not assets.
  3. In Awake, each equip button adds itself to the Button component's onClick. If Equip is also in the On Click list, each click equips twice.
  4. On click, the button finds its LoadoutTarget (its own target field if set, otherwise the nearest parent) and calls EquipGun, EquipTool, or EquipPassive.
  5. LoadoutTarget passes the choice to the player, then raises Changed.
  6. Every button and LoadoutReadout listening to Changed refreshes: buttons turn their optional equippedMarker child on or off, and the readout writes the equipped names into its text labels.

For a second player, duplicate the whole menu and point the copy's LoadoutTarget at player 2. The copy's tool buttons still reference player 1's tool components.

Custom Inspectors in LoadoutMenu/Editor/LoadoutMenuEditors.cs draw a help box with setup steps on each of these components, so teammates can wire up a menu without reading the scripts.

docs.text: The only scene with a loadout menu at v0.1.0 is Assets/Equipment/LoadoutMenu/Test.unity. It contains Player.prefab, a ProjectileManager, and a menu panel with equip buttons. One of its tool buttons points at a deleted asset.

docs.title: Passives
docs.text:
A Passive asset stores a description, a buff, a debuff, and a StatModifyMode. Its custom Inspector (PassiveEditor) spells out the intended rules:

  • buff is a positive change to a stat and debuff is a negative one.
  • Flat adds or subtracts the value directly; Percent scales the stat by that percentage.
  • A passive that switches on a behavior instead of changing a number keeps both values at 0, and other scripts check whether it's equipped.

PassiveHolder stores the equipped passive. The loadout menu reads it back for its markers and labels. No gameplay code reads it, so equipping a passive has no effect on play.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

The player is a zero-gravity Rigidbody2D that accelerates in the direction you hold, glides to a stop when you let go, and can brake to a dead stop and then relaunch at the speed it had. It has three hit points and a short invincibility window after each hit. In co-op, a dead player turns into a ghost that a teammate can revive.

  • Folder: Assets/Player/
  • Namespace: PlayerSystem (except PlayerAiming and PlayerAnimator)
  • Tuning: PlayerStats asset

docs.title: Movement
docs.text:
PlayerController reads PlayerInputHandler.Move in Update and applies forces in FixedUpdate. The input vector is normalized, so diagonals accelerate exactly as fast as cardinal directions, and a half-tilted stick counts as a full tilt.

Each physics step works like this:

  1. Holding a direction: if the player was at rest and wasn't holding anything last step, apply a one-time Impulse to get moving. Then add Acceleration as a continuous force. The first step of input also plays the jetpack start sound.
  2. Not holding anything: push against the current velocity with Deceleration. Because the push is capped so it can't overshoot, the player slides to an exact stop instead of jittering past zero. If the player is still moving on the first step after letting go, the jetpack end sound plays.
  3. Either way: clamp speed to MaxVelocity.

The clamp runs at the end of FixedUpdate, but Unity applies the forces added during the step (thrust, the starting impulse, recoil) after it. So the player can go slightly over the cap. While holding a direction at top speed, they cruise at MaxVelocity + Acceleration / Mass x 0.02, which is 8.4 units/s with the shipped values. The next step clamps them back down before adding thrust again.

linearDamping is forced to 0 in Awake, so the only thing that slows the player is the deceleration force.

docs.title: Braking and Relaunch
docs.text:
The brake stops the player dead, holds them in place, and throws them back out at their old speed in whatever direction they're holding when they let go.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Moving
    Moving --> Braking : Brake pressed (speed is saved)
    Braking --> Relaunch : Brake released
    Relaunch --> Moving : direction held (velocity = direction x saved speed)
    Relaunch --> Moving : 8 physics steps pass with no direction held
    note right of Braking : velocity forced to 0 every step
  • On press, the current speed is saved if it's above 0.1.
  • While held, velocity is set to zero every physics step.
  • On release, the player has 8 physics steps (0.16 s at the project's 0.02 s fixed timestep) to hold a direction. The first step with input sets velocity to that direction times the saved speed.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
PlayerInputHandler is the only script that talks to the Input System. It reads the Player action map of the PlayerInput component on the same object, and it exposes input in gameplay terms. Because every player prefab has its own PlayerInput, each player gets its own devices with no extra code.

Action Exposed as Read by Move Move property PlayerController Brake IsBrakeHeld, WasBrakePressedThisFrame, WasBrakeReleasedThisFrame PlayerController Fire FirePressed event PrimaryGun UseTool UseToolPressed event ToolUser UseToolAlt UseToolAltPressed event, raised after the button is held for the Input System's default hold time (0.4 s) ToolUser Aim + Point GetAimDirection(origin) PlayerAiming, RotateArmToAim Previous / Next Not exposed Nothing yet

GetAimDirection checks the active control scheme. On Keyboard&Mouse it returns the direction from origin to the cursor's world position (through Camera.main). On a gamepad it returns the right stick direction. When the stick is centered it keeps returning the last direction, so the arm doesn't snap back to the right.

docs.title: Aiming
docs.text:
Two scripts rotate arms toward the aim direction:

  • RotateArmToAim sits on the Arm Rotate Point object in Player.prefab. This is the one gameplay uses. The gun fires along this arm, and tools read its AimDirection. It's documented with Weapons and Projectiles.
  • PlayerAiming sits on the art in Player - Scope, and it's visual only. It runs in LateUpdate with [DefaultExecutionOrder(100)] so it rotates after PlayerAnimator flips the player. It rotates in the parent's local space so the arm stays correct while the player is mirrored.

docs.title: Health, Death, and Ghosts
docs.text:
PlayerHealth implements IDamageable. A hit plays the hurt sound, subtracts DamageAmount, and starts IframeDuration seconds of invincibility (often called i-frames). A hit that doesn't kill also calls PlayerController.PlayerDamaged(), which knocks DamageSpeedDecrease off the current speed, or off the saved brake speed while braking or relaunching. A hit for 0 damage still does all of this except subtracting health.

At 0 health, PlayerDeath.Die() stops the player and then branches on PlayerRegistry.IsMultiplayer:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Alive
    Alive --> GameOver : 0 HP, single player
    Alive --> GameOver : 0 HP, every player dead
    Alive --> Ghost : 0 HP, a teammate is alive
    Ghost --> Alive : touches a living player (revive at ReviveHealth)
    Ghost --> Removed : touches an object tagged Finish
    GameOver --> [*]
    Removed --> [*]
    note right of GameOver : stub at v0.1.0, see Known Issues

A ghost drifts in a straight line (down by default) and stops colliding with the layers in layersToIgnore (the Asteroid layer on the prefab). Its speed starts at BaseGhostSpeed and grows by DeathSpeedIncrease each further time that same player dies.

Only movement stops while a player is dead. PlayerController skips its Update and FixedUpdate while IsAlive is false, but PrimaryGun and ToolUser don't check it. See Known Issues.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
• Single-player game over does nothing. GameOver() only clears ghost state. The dead player stops moving and the fight keeps going.
  • Dead players can still shoot. PrimaryGun and ToolUser don't check IsAlive, so a dead player or a ghost can fire and throw bombs. With PlayerController skipped there's no deceleration or speed cap, so recoil leaves a dead player drifting.
  • Ghosts are never removed in MasterScene. Touching an object tagged Finish removes a ghost, but nothing in MasterScene has that tag, including the Factory Boss, so ghosts drift off-screen forever.
  • Co-op can't start from MasterScene. The scene has one player and no PlayerInputManager, so a second player has to be placed by hand to test co-op.
  • Two PlayerData tooltips are wrong. Impulse says "Not currently used", but PlayerController uses it. Mass says it doesn't affect acceleration, but acceleration and the starting impulse are both divided by mass. Only deceleration ignores it.
  • A saved brake speed can linger. If you release the brake without holding a direction within 8 physics steps, the player stays stopped and keeps the saved speed. The next brake from a standstill doesn't overwrite it, so the next relaunch uses the old speed.

docs.title: Differs from the GDD
docs.text:
• Brake. The GDD brake slows to a tenth of speed (bullet time), drains 33% of saved speed per second, costs 10% on repeated brakes, and relaunches toward the aim direction. The code stops dead, has no drain or cost, and relaunches toward the movement input.
  • Speed cap. The GDD discusses a soft cap where holding a direction keeps adding speed more slowly. The code clamps to MaxVelocity every step.
  • Getting hit. The GDD also displaces the player away from the attacker. The code only reduces speed.
  • Ghost speed. The GDD speeds ghosts up for every death in the match. The code tracks deaths per player.
  • Escape and terminal velocity aren't implemented. These are the GDD's two speed thresholds for ramming a boss: one to deal damage, one to kill it outright. The GDD rule that touching a boss below escape velocity damages the player isn't implemented either.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Accurate as of Milestone 1 (v0.1.0)

This page describes the game at release v0.1.0 (commit e3d0779, 2026-11-08). Source links point at that release, so they keep matching this page even after main moves on.

A tool is the equipment on right click. The GDD and some older code call this the Misc slot; players see "tool". Every tool is a Tool component with a cooldown, and ToolUser forwards the two tool buttons to whichever Tool is equipped. The Bomb Thrower is the only tool at v0.1.0. Grapples, magnets, and portals come later.

  • Folder: Assets/Equipment/Tools/
  • Namespace: global
  • Tuning: tools

docs.title: How It's Put Together
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction TB
    class ToolUser {
        +SetTool(tool)
    }
    class Tool {
        <<abstract>>
        #ToolData data
        +Use()
        +UseAlt()
        #OnUse()*
    }
    class ProjectileTool {
        <<abstract>>
        #ToolProjectileData projectileData
        #Fire() ToolProjectile
    }
    class BombThrower
    class ToolProjectile {
        <<abstract>>
        +ToolProjectileData Data
        +event Finished
        +Init(data, direction)
        #Finish()
    }
    class Bomb
    class ToolData {
        <<ScriptableObject>>
    }

        <<ScriptableObject>>
    }

    }

    Tool <|-- ProjectileTool
    ProjectileTool <|-- BombThrower
    Tool --> ToolData
    ProjectileTool --> ToolProjectileData
    ToolProjectile <|-- Bomb
    ToolProjectileData <|-- BombData
    Bomb --> BombData
